title: request dispatch backpressure scratchpad
content:
Context and goal:
This is a working scratchpad capturing an investigation into sporadic tail latency spikes observed on small payload RPCs (median token count < 16). Symptoms point to CPU-side dispatch/backpressure interactions rather than model inference itself. Goal: identify the dominant CPU hotpaths, reproduce in a minimal harness, and produce low-friction mitigations (short-term config changes + one medium-term runtime refactor).

High-level hypothesis (what we think is happening):
- Under moderate request rates (~200–600 rps per core), many small requests accumulate in the local run-queues and a central dispatch queue.
- The request dispatcher applies a spin-then-yield handoff (spin for Xµs then enqueue), which interacts poorly with the Python worker thread pool and the GIL — causing bursts where workers are starved waiting for parse/tokenize work to be dispatched.
- Tokenization + JSON header parsing is nontrivial: UTF-8 scanning + regex-ish heuristics take ~20–40µs per request on our benchmark VMs; when combined with dispatcher stalls we see 99.9p latency amplification.

Experiments run (quick log):
1) Minimal harness to reproduce
- harness: bench/small-req-harness.py (local) — sends synthetic JSON requests with 3–12 tokens, randomized whitespace and emojis to exercise unicode path.
- cluster: 4x c6g.4xlarge (arm64) dev nodes, runtime build: opt+sanity flags, pyshim enabled.
- baseline: 300 rps target, 8 worker threads
Result: p50 3.2ms, p95 10.8ms, p99 45ms, p99.9 320ms (sporadic).

2) Flame sampling (perf + py-spy) during spike windows
- top CPU sources (aggregate over spike windows):
  - request_dispatch_loop (C) 34%
  - tokenization/token_scan (Rust/Python FFI) 26%
  - json_parse_headers (C extension) 12%
  - cv.wait / condvar contention (pthread) 9%
  - syscall / futex wait 6%
  - Python GIL hold / interpreter frames 8%
Notes: many of the tokenization frames aggregate to a small set of functions that perform UTF-8 boundary scanning and token id mapping. The dispatch loop shows long runs where it is repeatedly waking workers but they don't take the work because they are preoccupied with other small syscall/windows.

3) Threadpool config sweep
- vary worker_count (N): 4, 8, 16 and dispatcher_spin_ms: 0, 50, 200
- observation: too few workers -> obvious queueing, too many -> context-switch cost increases but reduces 99.9p. Optimal at N ~= #vCPUs*0.7 for this workload.
- dispatcher_spin_ms: 0 (immediate yield) reduced p99 but increased CPU by ~6%; spin_ms=200 caused biggest spikes.

4) Tokenizer micro-optimizations (A/B)
- A: switch unicode scanning loop to chunked memchr-like scan (Rust) -> ~1.4x speedup on microbench
- B: pre-allocated token buffer reuse vs alloc per request -> modest wins for high rps
Outcome: combined A+B reduced tokenization cost from ~30µs to ~18µs on bench VM; spikes still present (reduced magnitude).

Key observations and pain points:
- Dispatch backpressure is emergent: when dispatcher decides to throttle/burst it creates a transient livelock between dispatcher and workers. The handoff is not strictly FIFO, so hot workers can be starved by frequent enqueuing cycles.
- Python overhead is not the largest absolute cost, but GIL interactions amplify the effect of small scheduling jitter. We saw GIL hold times occasionally spike when tokenizer and header parsing are executed in native extension code that reacquires the GIL or performs Python callbacks.
- Syscall frequency: small requests cause many short-lived syscalls (~3–6 per request) which increases scheduler noise at high rps. Batching syscalls (coalescing writes, reserved I/O buffers) helps but is not a silver bullet.

Repro steps to iterate locally:
1) checkout branch dispatch-probe
2) build runtime: ./build/release --enable-pyshim
3) run harness: python3 bench/small-req-harness.py --target-rps 350 --workers 8 --duration 300
4) collect perf samples: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 120; sudo perf script > out.stacks
5) py-spy: py-spy top --native --pid <pid>
6) trace wakeups: sudo trace-cmd record -e sched_wakeup -e sched_wakeup_new -e sched_switch -o wake.dat -- <command>

Quick mitigation checklist (short term):
- Set dispatcher_spin_ms=0 in prod for small-request-heavy routes (avoid spin-yield cycles).
- Tune worker_count to ~0.7 * vcpus for small-payload endpoints; add an autoscaling rule keyed on p99 latency.
- Enable token buffer pooling in current release (feature flag) to reduce alloc churn.
- For small-request-only routes, enable syscall coalescing (batch header write + single read) to reduce scheduler noise.

Medium term refactor ideas:
- Replace central dispatch with NUMA-aware sharded run-queues pinned to cores; keep local fastpath for cold-started requests and only fallback to central queue on overload.
- Rework tokenizer to be GIL-free in the hot loop: push UTF-8 scanning entirely to Rust worker and only return high-level token ids; avoid Python callbacks during scanning.
- Implement request prioritization that prefers requests already in worker-local queues to avoid repeated wake/race cycles.

Risk assessment and tradeoffs:
- Turning off dispatcher spin reduces tail but increases CPU. This increases cost for hosted tenants if applied cluster-wide. Need per-route config.
- GIL-free tokenizer requires careful FFI surface redesign; possible memory safety and UTF corner-case regressions. Must add extensive fuzzing and e2e evals.

Open questions to resolve:
- Are the spikes correlated with GC cycles in Python processes? We saw some overlap but not enough to explain magnitude.
- How much of the real traffic includes unicode-heavy payloads? Bench uses emojis -> may over-emphasize UTF paths. We need sample traces from production (anonymized) for distribution analysis. (See linked ticket SRV-3421 for log capture plan.)

Next steps (owner assigned):
- 1 week: Ravi to roll dispatcher_spin_ms=0 on canary small-req routes and collect metrics (Ravi).
- 2 weeks: Sofia to land token buffer pooling PR behind feature flag and run perf regression (Sofia).
- 4 weeks: Evelyn + Liam to prototype sharded run-queue design in a branch and validate with harness (Evelyn, Liam).

Notes to self / scratch fragments:
- Consider a cooperative worker token: dispatcher hands a token object to a worker to avoid enqueue-dequeue churn; token reused when request flow steady.
- Look at Linux futex wait/wake batching heuristics deeper; modern kernels sometimes coalesce wakes but we may be hitting edge cases.
- Add a lightweight event counter to dispatch path to rate-limit wake calls per-ms.

Appendix: quick numbers (from a representative run)
- harness config: 350 rps, 8 workers, 4 vCPUs
- p50: 3.2ms, p95: 10.8ms, p99: 42ms, p99.9: 320ms
- CPU breakdown (average during spike window): dispatch loop 34%, tokenization 26%, header parse 12%, condvar wait 9%, syscalls 6%, other 13%

Contact / references:
- Slack: #eng-serving-runtime (thread: dispatch-backpressure)
- Jira: SRV-3421 (captures traces)

End of scratchpad.
